bonus_mechanics: Virginia disallows federal bonus depreciation. Recompute depreciation for Virginia as if no bonus had been claimed (regular MACRS on the full basis). If the Virginia total is less than the federal deduction, add the difference to federal AGI; in later years, when the Virginia deduction exceeds the federal one, subtract the difference. No spread over years: the addition is the whole difference in the year of the claim.
change_note: 2022 session advanced the fixed date from 2020-12-31 to 2021-12-31 (Tax Bulletin 22-1, 23 Feb 2022) so ARPA flows through; the bonus-depreciation exception was unchanged.
special_rules: The exception covers bonus allowed under IRC 168(k), 168(l), 168(m), 1400L and 1400N. Keep a separate Virginia depreciation schedule and Virginia basis; gain or loss on sale uses the Virginia basis. 179 flows through to the Virginia return at the federal limit (federal dollar figures carried from docs/tax-research/depreciation-macrs-179-bonus-280f-2021-2026.md, not re-derived).

Tax Bulletin 16-1 (5 Feb 2016) https://www.tax.virginia.gov/laws-rules-decisions/tax-bulletins/16-1 (179 flows through at the indexed PATH Act limit). Va. Code 58.1-301 B https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title58.1/chapter3/section58.1-301/

bonus_mechanics: Not applicable: Washington has no individual income tax and no corporate income tax. The business and occupation (B&O) tax is a gross-receipts tax with no deduction for depreciation or other costs, so federal depreciation (bonus, 179, MACRS) never enters a Washington computation for a sole proprietor, pass-through owner or rental owner.
change_note: None for 2021. (The capital gains excise tax, RCW 82.87, applies to gains from 2022 on; ESSB 5096 enacted 2021.)
special_rules: No Washington depreciation adjustment. B&O: 'Because it is based on gross income, businesses cannot deduct expenses such as labor, materials, taxes, or other costs of doing business.'

bonus_mechanics: Not applicable: no individual or corporate income tax; B&O is a gross-receipts tax with no depreciation deduction. Capital gains excise tax (RCW 82.87, 7%) starts with 2022 gains but exempts real estate and 'assets used in a trade or business to the extent those assets are depreciable under 26 U.S.C. 167(a)(1) ... or qualify for expensing under 26 U.S.C. 179'.

For other capital assets the tax starts from federal net long-term capital gain per the code as of 2021-07-25 (RCW 82.87.020).

bonus_mechanics: Wisconsin has not adopted federal bonus depreciation: 'bonus depreciation is not allowed for Wisconsin purposes' and depreciation, depletion and amortization are computed under the IRC as in effect on 2014-01-01 (which has no bonus after 2013). Compute a Wisconsin-only depreciation schedule on the Wisconsin basis (regular MACRS, plus any Wisconsin 179). The difference between federal depreciation (with bonus) and Wisconsin depreciation is an addition on Schedule I for the year claimed, and Schedule I is adjusted again each later year until the asset is fully depreciated for both federal and Wisconsin purposes (later years usually produce a subtraction).
change_note: IRC definition for 2021 returns: IRC enacted as of 2020-12-31 with exceptions (2021 Schedule I instructions, per search summary).
special_rules: Wisconsin follows 'the same maximum dollar and business income limitations allowed for federal tax purposes' for 179 and the 179 election may differ from the federal one (complete a Wisconsin-only federal Form 4562 marked 'Revised for Wisconsin' and attach it to the Wisconsin return). 179 is claimed before any bonus. Disallowed 179 carries forward (income limit). Keep a separate Wisconsin basis; gain or loss on disposition uses it. Federal dollar limits carried from docs/tax-research/depreciation-macrs-179-bonus-280f-2021-2026.md.

special_rules: 179 follows 'federal law in effect for federal purposes for the year in which the property is placed in service' and the slides say Wisconsin 'adopts future annual adjustments for inflation', so the federal 2026 figures (Rev. bonus_mechanics: Not applicable: Wyoming imposes no individual income tax and no corporate income tax, so there is no state depreciation computation for a sole proprietor, pass-through owner or rental owner. Federal depreciation stands alone.
change_note: None found.
special_rules: Wyoming's taxes are ad valorem (property), mineral severance, sales/use and fuel/excise; none start from federal taxable income. Property-tax valuation of business equipment was not researched and is not a federal-depreciation conformity question.
